title: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List
directAnswer: Run two pointers from the head: slow moves one node per step, fast moves two. If there's a cycle, fast laps slow and they land on the same node — return true. If fast (or fast.next) reaches null, the list ends, so there's no cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space — no hash set needed.

remember.formula:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow is fast: return True
return False
rules: Guard **both** `fast` and `fast.next` before advancing fast two steps — skip either and you null-dereference (the named trap).
Move slow by 1 and fast by 2, then compare. Comparing before moving makes them 'equal' at the start and falsely reports a cycle.
Compare by **identity** (`slow is fast`), never by value — repeated values aren't a loop.
If the loop exits via the `while` condition, fast hit the end → **no cycle**, return false.
Do **not** modify the list (no marking visited via mutation) — it must stay read-only.
whenToUse: Decide whether a linked list loops back on itself
O(1) extra space is required, ruling out a hash set
Finding a cycle's start, its length, or the middle of a list (same fast/slow skeleton)
Cycle detection in any 'functional graph' where each node has one successor
antiSignals: You also need every visited node recorded for other reasons → a hash set may be reused
Nodes carry no stable identity (e.g. value-copied) → identity comparison won't work
The structure has multiple out-edges per node → this is a general graph; use DFS/visited colors
You may freely mutate and prefer the simplest code → marking visited can be acceptable
remember.takeaway: Two pointers at different speeds will always collide inside a loop and always exit a finite list — that single idea detects cycles in O(1) space. The same tortoise-and-hare skeleton finds the cycle's entry, the list's middle, and duplicates in Find the Duplicate Number.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you know Floyd's fast/slow pointers, can argue why they must meet inside a cycle, and whether you null-guard fast.next before the double advance.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Advancing fast = fast.next.next without first checking fast and fast.next for null, causing a NullPointerException on lists with no cycle or an even number of nodes.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(1)-space fast/slow solution, explain the 'fast gains one node per step on slow so it must close any gap inside the loop' argument, and mention the hash-set baseline plus the cycle-start follow-up (Floyd's phase 2).

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list. A **cycle** exists if some node's `next` points back to an earlier node, so following `next` repeats forever.

Return `true` if the list contains a cycle, and `false` otherwise. Do not modify the list.
constraints: The cycle, if present, can start at any node (including the head)
Must run in O(1) extra space for the optimal solution
understanding: Each node has exactly one next pointer, so following next either ends at null (no cycle) or loops forever inside a ring of nodes (cycle). We must decide which, without altering the list and ideally without extra memory.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the cycle defined by a node pointing back, or by repeated values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: By a node's next pointing to an earlier node — structural identity. Repeated values do not imply a cycle, so I compare node references.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I use extra memory, or is O(1) space required?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll show the O(n)-space hash-set approach for clarity, then the O(1)-space fast/slow pointers, which is usually what's wanted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Am I allowed to modify the list (e.g. mark visited nodes)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — keep it read-only. Mutation-based marking would corrupt the input.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to return the cycle's starting node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Here we only return true/false. Finding the entry node is a known follow-up (Floyd's second phase).

examples.explanation: The last node points back to the node holding 2, forming a loop, so the pointers eventually meet.
Two nodes pointing in a ring; fast laps slow and they collide.
Single node ending in null — fast.next is null, the loop exits, no cycle.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Fast/slow pointers give O(1) space; a hash set is simpler to explain but O(n) memory.

approaches.name: Hash Set — Remember Visited Nodes (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first as the obvious answer, then improve the space with fast/slow pointers.
hints: How would you notice you've arrived at a node you've already stood on?
Store each node's identity as you walk. What does it mean if next leads to a node already stored?
If you reach null before re-seeing a node, the list is finite — no cycle.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited at most once and does O(1) average set work → O(n) time. The set can hold up to n node references → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
We walk the list and remember every node we've stood on; revisiting one means we've looped.

**Why store nodes, not values.** A cycle is a structural fact — some `next` points back to an earlier *node*. Storing values would misfire on lists with repeated numbers. The set holds node references (identity).

**The two ways the walk ends.** Either we step onto a node already in the set (we've come around a loop → return true), or we reach null (the list terminated → return false). Exactly one happens, so the algorithm always halts.

**Why we improve on it.** This is the most direct solution and easy to defend, but it spends O(n) memory. Floyd's pointers get the same answer in O(1) space, which is the usual target — so present this, then optimize.
approaches.insight: Cycle detection becomes 'have I seen this exact node before?' — the same remember-and-probe membership idea as Two Sum, applied to references.

dryRun.intro: Add each node to a set; stop when next leads to a node already present.

java.explanation: Holds visited node references — identity, not value.
add returns false if cur was already present → we've looped back.
Reached null without a repeat → finite list, no cycle.

python.explanation: Re-seeing a node means next pointed back to it — a cycle.

diagrams.title: Visited set grows until a repeat
diagrams.caption: Keys are visited node identities. Following next onto a present key signals the cycle.

pitfalls: Storing values instead of node references — false positives on repeated values.
Adding cur after the check but forgetting to advance cur — infinite loop on acyclic lists.
Treating O(n) space as acceptable when the interviewer wants O(1).

edgeCases.behavior: head is null; loop never runs → false.
Add n1, advance to null → false.

approaches.name: Floyd's Fast/Slow Pointers — Tortoise and Hare (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The O(1)-space answer they want. Name it 'tortoise and hare' and explain why the pointers must meet inside a loop.
hints: Imagine two runners on a track, one twice as fast. On a circular track, what eventually happens to the gap between them?
Move slow one node and fast two nodes each step. Inside a cycle, fast closes the gap to slow by exactly one node per step — so it can't jump over without landing on it.
If there's no cycle, fast runs off the end. What two things must you null-check before doing fast = fast.next.next?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Without a cycle, fast reaches the end in n/2 steps. With a cycle of length L, once slow enters the loop fast catches it within L steps. Total O(n). Only two pointers → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We send a slow pointer (one step) and a fast pointer (two steps) from the head; a collision proves a cycle, and fast running off the end proves there isn't one.

**Why they must meet inside a cycle.** Once both pointers are inside the loop, consider the gap from fast to slow measured *forward around the ring*. Each step, slow advances 1 and fast advances 2, so fast gains exactly 1 on slow every step. A gap that shrinks by 1 each step inside a finite ring must hit 0 — and because it shrinks by exactly 1 (not 2 or more), fast can't leap over slow without landing on it. So they collide. This is why fast moves 2 and not 3: a larger stride could skip past slow on a small loop.

**Why no cycle terminates safely.** If the list ends, fast (the faster pointer) reaches null first. The loop condition `fast != null && fast.next != null` catches both the odd-length case (fast becomes null) and the even-length case (fast.next becomes null) before we ever dereference. Exit the loop → return false.

**The null-guard trap.** The single most common bug is `fast = fast.next.next` without first checking that `fast` and `fast.next` are non-null. On an acyclic list — or any list with an even node count — `fast.next` becomes null and `fast.next.next` throws. Both guards are mandatory, in that order (short-circuit).

**Compare by identity, and move before comparing.** The collision test is `slow == fast` on references. Also advance *then* compare: if you compare first, slow and fast both start at head and you'd wrongly report a cycle on step zero.
approaches.insight: Different speeds turn 'is there a loop?' into 'do two walkers collide?'. Because fast gains exactly one node per step, no gap inside a cycle can survive — the collision is guaranteed, and the finite list lets fast escape to null. The named trap is the missing fast.next null-check before the double hop.

dryRun.intro: slow +1, fast +2 each step. Compare AFTER moving. They collide inside the loop.

java.explanation: Guard BOTH fast and fast.next before the double hop — the named null trap.
Hare advances two; safe only because of the guards above.
Identity match means they've collided inside a cycle.
Loop exited because fast hit the end → no cycle.

python.line: while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
python.explanation: Both checks prevent a None dereference on fast.next.next.
Hare moves twice as fast to lap the tortoise inside any loop.
Compare by identity AFTER moving — comparing before would match at the start.
fast reached the end → list is finite, no cycle.

diagrams.title: Hare gains one node per step on the tortoise
diagrams.caption: Inside the loop the forward gap shrinks by exactly 1 each step, so the hare must land on the tortoise.

pitfalls: Writing fast = fast.next.next without guarding fast and fast.next — null dereference on acyclic or even-length lists.
Comparing slow == fast before advancing — false 'cycle' on the very first check since both start at head.
Comparing values instead of node identity.
Moving fast by 3 (or more) instead of 2 — it can leap over slow on a small loop and miss the collision.

edgeCases.behavior: fast is null; loop condition false immediately → false.
slow→2, fast→2.next.next: fast.next is null after one step → loop exits → false.
slow→1, fast→1 (1.next.next = 1) → slow is fast → true.

commonMistakes: Dereferencing fast.next.next without null-checking fast and fast.next first.
Comparing the pointers before moving them, reporting a cycle on step zero.
Comparing node values instead of node identity.
Using O(n) extra space when O(1) was the goal.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the fast.next null guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Advancing fast two steps requires both fast and fast.next to exist. On an acyclic list (or any even-length one) fast.next becomes null, and fast.next.next throws a null dereference.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing before moving
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Both pointers start at head, so an equality check before the first move is trivially true and reports a cycle on a list that has none.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while fast and fast.next:
    if slow is fast:        # true on entry — false positive
        return True
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next

followupVariations.hint: After the collision, reset one pointer to head and advance both by one — they meet at the cycle's entry.

followupVariations.hint: Same fast/slow skeleton: when fast reaches the end, slow sits on the middle.

patternNote: Floyd's tortoise-and-hare: two pointers at different speeds collide inside any cycle and escape any finite list, all in O(1) space. The same skeleton finds the cycle's entry, the list's middle, and duplicates in a functional graph.
